claims.text: In a full-text Google Scholar search conducted on August 5, 2024 for 'LLM' and 'content moderation', 844 out of 1220 results contained the keyword 'accuracy'.
Content moderation is a constitutive part of platform governance whose primary purpose is to gain and enhance legitimacy.
Accuracy is an insufficient metric for content moderation because it fails to distinguish between easy cases and hard cases.
Evaluating the moderation of easy cases requires metrics of accuracy, speed, and transparency.
Evaluating the moderation of hard cases requires metrics of reasoned justification and user participation.
Prompting LLMs with multiple content moderation policies simultaneously decreases classification accuracy.
Prompting LLMs with multiple content moderation policies simultaneously increases computational costs.

evidence.description: The author conducted a full-text search on Google Scholar on Aug 5, 2024 using keywords 'LLM' and 'content moderation' and manually verified that roughly two-thirds (844 of 1220) contained 'accuracy'.
Platform moderation limits fundamental rights without democratic authorization or constitutional mandate, making normative legitimacy essential to justify private governance power.
In hard cases involving complex factual contexts, rule vagueness, rule plurality, or value conflicts, intercoder human disagreement shows there is no objective 'ground truth' standard for accuracy.
Cites Thomas et al. (2024, pp. 9-10) demonstrating that LLM classification accuracy decreases when prompted with multiple moderation policies.
Cites Thomas et al. (2024, pp. 9-10) demonstrating that processing long inputs containing tens of thousands of words of content rules increases LLM moderation costs.

methodologies.name: Legitimacy-based framework for evaluating LLM content moderation
methodologies.description: A socio-legal evaluation framework distinguishing easy and hard moderation cases and evaluating them against substantive (accuracy, speed, justification) and procedural (transparency, participation) legitimacy metrics.

methodologies.name: Collaborative human-LLM content moderation workflow
methodologies.description: A multi-tiered operational workflow integrating traditional ML classifiers for routine screening, LLMs for hard case filtering and rationale generation, and human/expert reviewers for escalated appeals and value decisions.

limitations.text: Traditional ML moderation relies heavily on manual annotation of training datasets, creating high labor costs and introducing human annotator bias.
Traditional ML moderation models lack adaptability to changing contexts or policies across different languages and cultures.
The existing literature on LLM content moderation focuses predominantly on single accuracy metrics while ignoring systematic platform governance legitimacy.
The proposed legitimacy-based framework and collaborative moderation workflow are conceptual and lack empirical testing in production platform environments.
LLM-generated moderation explanations remain susceptible to hallucinations, sycophancy, and geographical or political biases.

future_work.text: Empirically test the proposed legitimacy-based framework and refine the collaborative moderation workflow in real-world platform settings.
Improve prompting strategies and uncertainty quantification methods to enhance LLM reliability in distinguishing hard cases from easy cases.
Develop techniques to mitigate LLM hallucinations, sycophancy, and geographical/political biases in generated moderation explanations.
Design user-centric API interfaces and interactive affordances that facilitate user participation and contestation compliant with regulatory standards.
